name: Ersu
confidence_why: Zhang's 2013 reference grammar, the separate field team of Chirkova et al. 2015 and Chirkova & Wang 2017, and Yu's 2012 comparative dissertation all describe Ersu as a two-tone register language with no contrastive word stress; the only wrinkle is whether a word-final high pitch (Zhang 2013) or the marginal HL word pattern (Chirkova et al. 2015, tested by Elmerich et al. 2025) deserves the label 'stress-like', a question of phonetic labelling rather than of what kind of system Ersu has.

catalog_locator: Zhang 2013, Ch. 2 Phonology: §2.3 Tones, pp. 79-80; §2.4.1 General properties of phonological words, pp. 83-85 Chirkova et al. 2015 'Prosodic organization' pp. 205-207
catalog_quote: In Ersu, the tone-bearing unit is a syllable. Tones are closely associated with syllables and each syllable must bear a tone. There are two tones with contrastive minimal pairs found in Ersu: high level (formally unmarked in this grammar) and mid level [...] The assignment of the two tones to a particular morpheme or word is unpredictable. However, the data demonstrate that the syllables taking a high level tone are much more frequent than those taking a mid level tone. [pp. 79-80] [...] Secondly, tone sandhi is another criterion to sort out a phonological word in speech. Though the assignment of a tone to a syllable is unpredictable (§2. 3. 1), the combination of tones in a phonological word is predictable. [p. 83] [...] The final syllable of a trisyllabic or polysyllabic word often takes a mid level tone. This is quite effective in identifying a phonological word. [...] In addition, if the final syllable of a phonological word has a high level tone, it, as a word boundary, will sound much higher in context than in isolation. For example, a speaker tends to have the final syllable tsɿ of the word xitsɿ ‘rabbit’ stressed with a much higher pitch in speaking. On the other hand, if the final syllable of a phonological word has a mid level tone, it will sound much lower in realization than in isolation. [...] In addition, if the onset syllable of a word has a high level tone, it will most often slightly descend from high to low, sounding like a high falling tone. [p. 85]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ersu is a two-register tone language (high vs. mid/low, lexically unpredictable per syllable); no word-stress rule is given. Word-level prominence is tonal: in a phonological word the tone pattern is levelled (mid+high > high+high; the final syllable of longer words often mid), and a word-final high-tone syllable is realised with extra-high pitch ('stressed') as a boundary cue, while a word-initial high tone tends to fall. Chirkova et al. 2015 (JIPA, pp. 205-207) independently describe the same system as register tone with tone reduction on non-initial syllables (initial syllable keeps its tone), plus a marginal HL pattern whose second syllable 'sounds much less prominent.. giving rise to the impression that it is unstressed'; a 2025 instrumental test (Elmerich et al., abstract only) finds only partial support for stress-like prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Zhang: two marginal non-lexical tones (mid rising, falling-rising) on clause-final enclitics; final syllable of tri-/polysyllabic words often mid level; Liu 1983 reports five tones for the Liaoping subdialect. Chirkova et al. 2015: a marginal HL disyllabic pattern (Chinese loanwords, fusions, a few native words) with a perceptually unstressed second syllable; LL vs LH in free variation.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (compounds, affixed and cliticised words) in connected speech; tones cited in isolation forms. Zhang: Lajigu subdialect, Ganluo county. Chirkova et al.: Ganluo Ersu, instrumental (wordlist and text).
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand sources describe Ersu proper (ersu1241), Ganluo county: Zhang 2013 the Lajigu subdialect (Ganluo), Chirkova et al. 2015 Ganluo Ersu. The sister varieties Lizu (lizu1234) and Duoxu (duox1234), covered by Sun 1982 under 'Ersu (Duoxu)', are separate glottocodes and were not used. Liu 1983's Liaoping subdialect is reported to have five tones, unlike the two-tone Lajigu/Ganluo system.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on the type: every work opened for this language (Zhang 2013 and Chirkova et al. 2015 from the earlier reading, and now Chirkova & Wang 2017 and Yu 2012) describes Ersu as a two-tone register language with word-level tone patterns and none posits contrastive word stress. The only difference is one of framing, not fact: Zhang 2013 (§2.4.1, p. 85) calls the word-final H syllable of Lajigu Ersu 'stressed with a much higher pitch' as a word-boundary cue, whereas Chirkova & Wang 2017 (fn. 4) analyse the same word-final high on all-low words as a tonal prosodic-word boundary marker without using the notion of stress; Chirkova et al. 2015 (p. 207) likewise speak only of an 'impression' that the second syllable of HL words is unstressed, and Elmerich et al. 2025 (abstract) find only partial support for stress-like prominence. Yu 2012 additionally reduces Liu 1983's five Qingshui tones to two word-tones, a tonal not a stress matter.

sources.note: No stress section and no word-stress rule. Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.3 Tones (pp. 79-80): two lexically unpredictable register tones (high level, mid level) plus two marginal enclitic tones; §2.4.1 (pp. 83-85): tone sandhi delimits the phonological word (mid+high > high+high in disyllables; final syllable of tri-/polysyllabic words often mid level), and a word-final high-tone syllable is 'stressed with a much higher pitch' as a boundary cue while a word-initial high tone tends to fall. Lajigu subdialect, Ganluo county.

sources.note: 'Prosodic organization' (pp. 205-207): Ersu is a register tone language with two registers, L and H; in polysyllabic domains the domain-initial syllable retains its tone and non-initial syllables undergo tone reduction (HH, LL/LH, and a marginal HL pattern). Of the HL pattern (mostly Chinese loans, fusions, a few native words): 'the second syllable of these words sounds much less prominent than the first syllable, giving rise to the impression that it is unstressed' (p. 207). No word-stress rule is stated. Ganluo Ersu; instrumental.
